claim: During chemotaxis in the Drosophila melanogaster larva, the detection of positive odor gradients extends runs while negative gradients promote stops and turns.
source: During chemotaxis in the Drosophila melanogaster larva, the detection of positive odor gradients extends runs while negative gradients promote stops and turns.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational principle of larval chemotaxis behavior.

claim: PDM-DN is an olfactory descending neuron that plays a pivotal role in the organization of stops and turns in response to the detection of graded changes in odor concentrations.
source: In the present work, we identified an olfactory descending neuron, PDM-DN, which plays a pivotal role in the organization of stops and turns in response to the detection of graded changes in odor concentrations.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Artificial activation of PDM-DN induces deterministic stops followed by the initiation of turning maneuvers through head casts.
source: Artificial activation of this descending neuron induces deterministic stops followed by the initiation of turning maneuvers through head casts.
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3 and Video 1.

claim: The main pathway connecting PDM-DN to the peripheral olfactory system and to the pre-motor circuit responsible for forward peristalsis was reconstructed using electron microscopy.
source: Using electron microscopy, we reconstructed the main pathway that connects the PDM-DN neuron to the peripheral olfactory system and to the pre-motor circuit responsible for the actuation of forward peristalsis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by EM reconstruction data in Figures 2, 5, and 7.

claim: Bacteria efficiently ascend gradients of attractive chemicals by extending their runs toward positive gradients.
source: In spite of the undirected nature of reorientation through tumbling, bacteria efficiently ascend gradients of attractive chemicals (e.g., sugar) by extending their runs toward positive gradients.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in bacterial chemotaxis cited from the literature (Berg, 2008; Bi and Sourjik, 2018).

claim: C. elegans and D. melanogaster larvae suppress turning during up-gradient runs, but turning is facilitated during down-gradient runs.
source: Similarly, the nematode C. elegans and the D. melanogaster larva suppress turning during up-gradient runs, but turning is facilitated during down-gradient runs (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999; Lockery, 2011; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Adult flies walk upwind when stimulated by an attractive odor, and termination of odor stimulations elicits stops and reversals in walking adult flies.
source: Adult flies walk upwind when stimulated by an attractive odor. Termination of odor stimulations elicits stops and reversals in walking adult flies (DasGupta et al., 2014; Bell and Wilson, 2016; Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on adult fly behavior.

claim: Flying insects such as pheromone-seeking male moths and foraging adult flies respond to attractive olfactory cues by implementing upwind 'surges', and exiting the odor plume triggers searches through casting behavior.
source: Flying insects such as pheromone-seeking male moths and foraging adult flies respond to attractive olfactory cues by implementing upwind 'surges'. Exiting the odor plume triggers searches through casting behavior (Murlis et al., 1992; Bhandawat et al., 2010; van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on insect flight behavior.

claim: Drosophila larvae display robust orientation behavior in response to food odors.
source: Drosophila larvae display robust orientation behavior in response to food odors (Cobb, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Larval chemotaxis results from coordinated transitions between four behavioral primitives: runs, stops, head casts, and turns.
source: Larval chemotaxis results from coordinated transitions between four behavioral primitives: runs (forward motion by means of symmetrical peristaltic contractions), stops (cessation of peristaltic waves), head casts (lateral head sweeps) and turns (asymmetrical contractions of the body segments followed by straightening of the body) (Green et al., 1983; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies that characterized larval behavior.

claim: Larvae time the initiation of reorientation maneuvers based on the detection of negative sensory gradients.
source: To accurately navigate attractive odor gradients, larvae implement two sensorimotor tasks: they time the initiation of reorientation maneuvers based on the detection of negative sensory gradients (Figure 1Ai)
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1Ai and previous studies (Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012).

claim: Larvae direct turns toward the local odor gradient.
source: and they direct turns toward the local odor gradient (Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Acute activations of olfactory sensory neurons through optogenetics have established quantitative relationships between the activity of the peripheral olfactory system and the release of specific motor programs such as stops.
source: Acute activations of olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) through optogenetics have established quantitative relationships between the activity of the peripheral olfactory system and the release of specific motor programs such as stops prior to the initiation of reorientation maneuvers (Gepner et al., 2015; Hernandez-Nunez et al., 2015; Schulze et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous optogenetic studies.

claim: Nonlinear aspects of the input-output response properties of larval OSNs are essential to explain how dynamic patterns of stimulus intensity evoke predictable and stereotypical sequences of behavioral control.
source: Nonlinear aspects of the input-output response properties of the larval OSNs are essential to explain how dynamic patterns of stimulus intensity evoke predictable and stereotypical sequences of behavioral control (Schulze et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The larval olfactory system comprises only 21 olfactory sensory neurons.
source: The larval olfactory system is compact: it comprises only 21 olfactory sensory neurons (OSN) (Fishilevich et al., 2005; Kreher et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The axon terminals of OSNs synapse onto second-order projection neurons (PNs) in the antennal lobe.
source: The axon terminals of OSNs synapse onto second-order projection neurons (PNs) in the antennal lobe (AL).
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about the larval olfactory system.

claim: The anatomical organization of the larval antennal lobe has been characterized through a combination of light and electron microscopy.
source: The anatomical organization of the larval AL has been characterized through a combination of light and electron microscopy (Ramaekers et al., 2005; Masuda-Nakagawa et al., 2009; Berck et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The axons of PNs project to two main neuropil centers in the larval brain lobes: the lateral horn and the mushroom body.
source: The axons of the PNs project to two main neuropil centers in the larval brain lobes where further sensory processing takes place: the lateral horn (LH) and the mushroom body (MB).
evidence: This is a well-established anatomical fact about the larval olfactory system.

claim: The entire connectome of the larval mushroom body has been reconstructed using electron microscopy.
source: The entire connectome of the larval MB has been reconstructed using electron microscopy (Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In adult Drosophila, PN axons arising from the same glomerulus of the antennal lobe converge onto stereotyped and overlapping regions of the lateral horn.
source: In the adult Drosophila, PN axons arising from the same glomerulus of the AL converge onto stereotyped and overlapping regions of the LH (Marin et al., 2002; Wong et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies in adult flies.

claim: Distinct odors trigger calcium responses in specific regions of the lateral horn in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Distinct odors trigger calcium responses in specific regions of the LH in a way that is concentration-dependent (Strutz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Pre-motor circuits located in the ventral nerve cord are responsible for generating patterns of rhythmic motor activities that create peristaltic motion through stereotyped sequences of muscle contractions.
source: At the other end of the central nervous system of the larva, pre-motor circuits located in the ventral nerve cord (VNC) are responsible for generating patterns of rhythmic motor activities that create peristaltic motion through stereotyped sequences of muscle contractions (Inada et al., 2011; Berni et al., 2012; Kohsaka et al., 2012; Berni, 2015; Pulver et al., 2015; Fushiki et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on larval motor circuits.

claim: Central pattern generating networks underlie the production of rhythmic motor output in the absence of sensory feedback or input from other brain regions.
source: Central pattern generating (CPG) networks underlie the production of rhythmic motor output in the absence of sensory feedback or input from other brain regions (Marder and Calabrese, 1996; Katz, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on CPG networks.

claim: Isolated larval central nervous systems are sufficient to produce segmentally-coordinated motor output, suggesting that CPGs underlying peristalsis are located in segmentally-organized network elements in the VNC.
source: The observation that isolated larval central nervous systems (CNS) are sufficient to produce segmentally-coordinated motor output suggests that the CPGs underlying peristalsis are located in segmentally-organized network elements in the VNC (Fox et al., 2006; Inada et al., 2011; Berni et al., 2012; Berni, 2015; Lemon et al., 2015; Pulver et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on isolated CNS preparations.

claim: Descending neural pathways create a bottleneck in sensorimotor transformations by creating an interface between circuits that carry out sensory processing in the brain lobes and those in charge of motor pattern generation in the VNC.
source: Descending neural pathways create a bottleneck in sensorimotor transformations: they create an interface between the circuits that carry out sensory processing in the brain lobes and those in charge of motor pattern generation in the VNC.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about the role of descending neurons in sensorimotor control.

claim: Descending neurons are often regarded as key elements of 'command' circuits that condition the release of naturally occurring motor programs.
source: Descending neurons are often regarded as key elements of 'command' circuits that condition the release of naturally occurring motor programs (Kristan, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on command neurons.

claim: In the leech, descending 'command' neurons with somas in the subesophageal zone integrate mechanosensory inputs to trigger segmental swim-initiating circuits in the VNC.
source: The leech provides a prime example of descending 'command' neurons with somas in the subesophageal zone (SEZ) where mechanosensory inputs are integrated to trigger segmental swim-initiating circuits in the VNC (Brodfuehrer and Friesen, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on leech descending neurons.

claim: In adult Drosophila, activation of distinct descending neurons can elicit stereotypic behaviors such as backward walking and courtship song.
source: In adult Drosophila, activation of distinct descending neurons can elicit stereotypic behaviors such as backward walking (Bidaye et al., 2014) and courtship song (von Philipsborn et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on adult fly descending neurons.

claim: Most descending neurons in adult Drosophila produce a single behavioral output, while a minority trigger multiple behavioral outputs that are manifested either simultaneously or sequentially.
source: Recently, a detailed analysis of a large collection of Split-Gal4 driver lines targeting distinct descending neuron populations has concluded that most descending neurons produce a single behavioral output, while a minority of descending neurons are sufficient to trigger multiple behavioral outputs that are manifested either simultaneously or sequentially (Cande et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on adult fly descending neurons.

claim: In the larva, descending inputs from the brain lobes and SEZ are necessary to regulate the speed and frequency of CPGs in charge of the actuation of forward runs, stop-turns, and backward runs.
source: In the larva, descending inputs from the brain lobes (BL) and SEZ are necessary to regulate the speed and frequency of the CPGs in charge of the actuation of forward runs, stop-turns and backward runs (Berni et al., 2012; Pulver et al., 2015; Tastekin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on larval descending neurons.

claim: A loss-of-function screen was conducted on a large collection of Split-Gal4 driver lines to identify neurons in the larval brain involved in chemotaxis behavior.
source: To identify neurons in the larval brain involved in chemotaxis behavior, we conducted a loss-of-function (LoF) screen on a large collection of Split-Gal4 driver lines (Li et al., 2014; Dionne et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Acute loss-of-function impairments were achieved by blocking synaptic transmission with tetanus toxin light chain.
source: Acute LoF impairments were achieved by blocking synaptic transmission with tetanus toxin light chain (TNT) (Sweeney et al., 1995).
evidence: This describes the method used to silence neurons in the screen.

claim: The screen was based on a modified version of a high-throughput olfactory assay using the multi-worm tracker to track orientation behavior of multiple larvae simultaneously.
source: The screen was based on a modified version of a high-throughput olfactory assay introduced in previous work (Tastekin et al., 2015). The spatio-temporal resolution of the loss-of-function characterization was enhanced by using the multi-worm tracker (MWT) (Swierczek et al., 2011), which allowed us to track orientation behavior of multiple larvae simultaneously in a single trial (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup used in the screen, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The behavioral assay consisted of a large square dish coated with agar with four hanging droplets of an attractive odor in the lid.
source: The assay consisted of a large square dish coated with agar. The lid of the dish was outfitted with four hanging droplets of an attractive odor (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Each of the four odor sources created a gradient that acted like a spatial attractor on the behavior of single larvae.
source: Each of the four odor sources created a gradient, which acted like a spatial attractor on the behavior of single larvae (Figure 1Biii and Figure 1Biv).
evidence: This describes the behavioral effect of the odor sources, with reference to Figure 1Biii and 1Biv.

claim: Twenty larvae were placed in the middle of the arena and tracked for 5 minutes.
source: We placed 20 larvae in the middle of the arena and tracked their trajectories for 5 min (Figure 1Bi and Figure 1Bii).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: The initial orientation of a larva was a key factor determining the source under which it resided.
source: We observed empirically that the initial orientation of a larva was a key factor determining the source under which it resided (Figure 1Biii and Figure 1Biv).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1Biii and 1Biv.

claim: Multiple sources were used to minimize interactions between individual larvae by distributing their accumulation across four regions of the plate.
source: Multiple sources were used to minimize interactions between individual larvae by distributing their accumulation across four regions of the plate (Figure 1Biii and Figure 1Biv).
evidence: This explains the rationale for using four odor sources in the assay.

claim: Approximately 300 Split-Gal4 driver lines were screened, most of which labeled only a single neuron per brain hemisphere.
source: We screened ~300 Split-Gal4 driver lines most of which labeled only a single neuron per brain hemisphere (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the scope of the screen.

claim: Silencing neurons labeled by eighteen different Split-Gal4 driver lines led to a statistically significant increase or decrease in chemotactic performances.
source: Silencing neurons labeled by eighteen different Split-Gal4 driver lines led to a statistically significant increase or decrease in chemotactic performances (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from the screen shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: A Split-Gal4 line was identified that specifically labels an olfactory descending neuron (PDM-DN) connecting the lateral horn region of the brain lobes to the ventral nerve cord.
source: This approach permitted the identification of a Split-Gal4 line that specifically labels an olfactory descending neuron (PDM-DN) connecting the lateral horn region of the brain lobes to the ventral nerve cord (Figure 1C and Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a key finding from the screen, shown in Figures 1C and 2A.

claim: The loss-of-function phenotype associated with PDM-DN silencing demonstrated an overall reduction in the accuracy of chemotaxis manifested as a wider spread of individual trajectories around the odor sources.
source: The LoF phenotype associated with the expression of TNT in PDM-DN (PDM-DN>TNT) demonstrated an overall reduction in the accuracy of chemotaxis manifested as a wider spread of individual trajectories around the odor sources (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the behavioral phenotype observed upon PDM-DN silencing, shown in Figure 1D.

claim: PDM-DN-silenced larvae remained further away from the odor source than their positive controls during the first three minutes of a trial.
source: During the first three minutes of a trial, PDM-DN>TNT larvae (Figure 1E, magenta trace) remained further away from the source than their positive controls (Figure 1E, black trace).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral assay shown in Figure 1E.

claim: While parental-control larvae stayed at an average distance of ~13 mm to the nearest source between 120 and 240 s, PDM-DN silenced larvae remained at a larger distance (~19 mm) during the same period.
source: While parental-control larvae stayed at an average distance of ~13 mm to the nearest source between 120 and 240 s, PDM-DN silenced larva remained at a larger distance (~19 mm) during the same period of time.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral assay.

claim: The loss-of-function defect of PDM-DN did not result from an overall decrease in locomotor speed.
source: The LoF defect did not result from an overall decrease in locomotor speed (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is a control result shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: PDM-DN silencing resulted in a significant decrease in turn rate.
source: but a significant decrease in turn rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: In spite of the significant turning defect, the ability of PDM-DN>TNT larvae to orient toward the odor gradient was sufficient to produce significant accumulation under the source compared to the no-odor control.
source: In spite of this significant turning defect, the ability of PDM-DN >TNT larvae to orient toward the odor gradient was sufficient to produce significant accumulation under the source compared to the no-odor control (Figure 1Biv and E and F).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data shown in Figures 1Biv, 1E, and 1F.

claim: The PDM-DN neurons form a pair of bilaterally symmetrical cells in each brain lobe.
source: The PDM-DN neurons form a pair of bilaterally symmetrical cells in each brain lobe (Figure 2Ai).
evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 2Ai.

claim: Each PDM-DN sends its dendrite and axon contralateral to its cell body.
source: By using the MultiColor FlpOut (MCFO) technique to reveal the anatomy of individual neurons (Nern et al., 2015), we showed that each PDM-DN sends its dendrite and axon contralateral to its cell body (Figure 2Aiv).
evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 2Aiv using the MCFO technique.

claim: The soma of PDM-DN is located in the posterior-dorsal-medial region of the brain.
source: The soma of PDM-DN is located in the posterior-dorsal-medial region of the brain (Figure 2Aii).
evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 2Aii.

claim: PDM-DN has dendritic arborizations around the mushroom body peduncle and near the lateral horn region, suggesting that PDM-DN receives olfactory input.
source: Closer inspection revealed that PDM-DN has dendritic arborizations around the mushroom body (MB) peduncle (the axonal bundle of Kenyon cells preceding the formation of the MB lobes) and near the lateral horn (LH) region, suggesting that PDM-DN receives olfactory input (Figure 2Aiii).
evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 2Aiii, with an inference about function.

claim: The axon of PDM-DN extends to the VNC dorso-medially and targets three regions: the subesophageal zone, the thoracic neuromeres, and the first four abdominal neuromeres.
source: The axon of PDM-DN extends to the VNC dorso-medially (Figure 2Ai, left inset) and targets three regions: the subesophageal zone (SEZ), the thoracic neuromeres and the first four abdominal neuromeres (Figure 2Ai).
evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 2Ai.

claim: PDM-DN was identified in the EM stack based on the unequivocal resemblance of the candidate neuron reconstructed from EM and light microscopy.
source: We identified PDM-DN in the EM stack based on the unequivocal resemblance of the candidate neuron reconstructed from the EM and light microscopy (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the method used to identify PDM-DN in the EM data.

claim: Ethyl butyrate predominantly activates two olfactory sensory neurons at moderate concentrations: Or42a and Or42b.
source: This odor predominantly activates two olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) at the moderate concentrations used in our LoF experiments: Or42a and Or42b (Kreher et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a fact about odor-receptor interactions supported by a citation.

claim: PDM-DN receives the strongest olfactory inputs from the Or42a and Or42b OSNs through the lateral horn region.
source: We traced the pre-synaptic partners of PDM-DN all the way up to the sensory periphery and found that PDM-DN receives the strongest olfactory inputs from the Or42a and Or42b OSNs through the lateral horn region (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The uniglomerular projection neurons downstream from the Or42a and Or42b OSNs directly innervate the local interneuron LH-LN1 in the lateral horn region.
source: The uniglomerular projection neurons (PNs) downstream from the Or42a and Or42b OSNs directly innervate the local interneuron LH-LN1 in the lateral horn region (Figure 2B–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figures 2B-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LH-LN1 receives ipsilateral input from olfactory projection neurons and sends axonal projections that bilaterally synapse onto PDM-DN and onto a second local interneuron in the lateral horn region, LH-LN2.
source: While LH-LN1 receives ipsilateral input from olfactory projection neurons, it sends axonal projections that bilaterally synapse onto PDM-DN and onto a second local interneuron in the lateral horn region, LH-LN2 (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figures 2B-C.

claim: LH-LN2 gives bilateral inputs to PDM-DN.
source: In addition, LH-LN2 gives bilateral inputs to PDM-DN (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The circuit motif encompassing LH-LN1, LH-LN2, and PDM-DN constitutes a feedforward motif downstream from the olfactory projection neurons.
source: The circuit motif encompassing LH-LN1, LH-LN2 and PDM-DN constitute a feed-forward motif (Alon, 2006) downstream from the olfactory projection neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the circuit connectivity with reference to a known circuit motif.

claim: Silencing PDM-DN compromised the ability of larvae to accurately locate the nearest odor source and to stay under this position in a single-odor-source assay.
source: Consistent with the results of group behavior tested in the four-odor-source assay (Figure 1D), a visual inspection of the trajectories of PDM-DN>TNT and its parental controls revealed that silencing the function of PDM-DN compromised the ability of larvae to accurately locate the nearest odor source and to stay under this position (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is a result from the single-larva tracking assay shown in Figures 3A-B.

claim: Both parental controls and PDM-DN>TNT larvae accumulate near the source after a transient phase (~30 s) during which larvae moved up the gradient.
source: By quantifying the orientation behavior through the distance to the source, we observed that both parental controls and the PDM-DN>TNT larvae accumulate near the source after a transient phase (~30 s) during which larvae moved up the gradient.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis.

claim: The average distance to the source of PDM-DN silenced larvae gradually increased after ~120 s while it remained stationary for both parental controls during ~240 s.
source: Unlike the results of the four-odor-source assay (Figure 1), the average distance to the source of the PDM-DN silenced larvae gradually increased after ~120 s (Figure 3C, magenta trace) while it remained stationary for both parental controls during ~240 s (Figure 3C, blue and black traces).
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Silencing PDM-DN did not significantly decrease the run speed of PDM-DN>TNT larvae compared to the slowest parental control.
source: This difference is unlikely to be explained by an overall reduction in locomotor activity given that silencing PDM-DN did not significantly decrease the run speed of PDM-DN>TNT larvae compared to the slowest parental control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and H).
evidence: This is a control result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and H.

claim: Significant differences in run speeds were observed between the two parental controls, likely caused by genetic background.
source: We nonetheless observed significant differences in the run speeds of the two parental controls — an effect likely caused by genetic background.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with an inference about the cause.

claim: PDM-DN>TNT larvae turned less frequently than either parental control in a time window during the middle of the experiment (120-180 s).
source: In agreement with the results of the four-odor-source assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we found that PDM-DN>TNT larvae turned less frequently than either parental control (Figure 3D, left).
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A difference in turn rates was only observed for down-gradient runs when turn rates were conditioned on the sensory experience of the larva.
source: We then conditioned the turn-rate analysis on the sensory experience of the larva: turn rates were measured separately for up-gradient and down-gradient runs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C). A difference in turn rates was only observed for down-gradient runs.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Silencing PDM-DN reduces the likelihood that larvae terminate runs associated with negative changes in odor concentration.
source: Therefore, we conclude that silencing PDM-DN reduces the likelihood that larvae terminate runs associated with negative changes in odor concentration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: The likelihood of turning during the up-gradient phase of a run was unaffected by the loss-of-function manipulation of PDM-DN.
source: By contrast, the likelihood of turning during the up-gradient phase of a run was unaffected by the LoF manipulation.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis.

claim: Silencing PDM-DN did not lead to a decrease in turn rate in the absence of odor gradients.
source: In addition, silencing of PDM-DN did not lead to a decrease in turn rate in the absence of odor gradients, supporting the idea that the PDM-DN LoF phenotype is not due to an overall decrease in run-to-turn transitions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is a control result shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Larvae with silenced PDM-DN displayed no decrease in the accuracy of the orientation of their turns.
source: Larvae with silenced PDM-DN displayed no decrease in the accuracy of the orientation of their turns.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis.

claim: One parental control showed a significant reduction in turning performances compared to PDM-DN>TNT and the other parental control.
source: Interestingly the parental control (SS01994 x w-/-) showed a significant reduction in turning performances compared of PDM-DN>TNT and the other parental control (Figure 3D, right panel).
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The decrease in reorientation performances of one parental control might be due to the higher locomotor speed displayed by this control, which might compromise the speed-accuracy tradeoff necessary to accurately sample and navigate odor space.
source: This decrease in reorientation performances might be due to the higher locomotor speed displayed by this parental control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), which might compromise the speed-accuracy tradeoff necessary to accurately sample and navigate odor space (Chittka et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data with reference to a general principle.

claim: Optogenetically-induced activation of PDM-DN produced a nearly deterministic switch from an ongoing run to a stop-turn.
source: Optogenetically-induced activation of PDM-DN produced a nearly deterministic switch from an ongoing run to a stop-turn (Video 1).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Video 1.

claim: The switch from running to stopping upon PDM-DN activation was highly reproducible.
source: The switch from running to stopping was highly reproducible (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: A series of 8 consecutive light flashes produced eight transitions from a run to a stop-turn.
source: A series of 8 consecutive light flashes produced eight transitions from a run (high-tail speed) to a stop-turn (low-tail speed) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Averaging the time course of tail-speed over 280 flashes yielded a stereotyped decrease in tail speed associated with the interruption of forward locomotion.
source: Averaging the time course of the tail-speed over 280 flashes yielded a stereotyped decrease in tail speed associated with the interruption of forward locomotion (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The non-zero value of the average tail speed resulted from inter-trial variability in the timing of stops.
source: The non-zero value of the average tail speed resulted from inter-trial variability in the timing of stops (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Negative parental controls only showed a modest decrease in tail speed likely arising from startle responses.
source: By contrast, negative parental controls only showed a modest decrease in tail speed that is likely to arise from startle responses.
evidence: This is a result from control experiments with an inference about the cause.

claim: The probability that wild-type controls stopped in response to light was nearly null and markedly lower than PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae.
source: The probability that wild-type controls stopped in response to light was nearly null and markedly lower than PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In few cases where wild-type larvae stopped, the average duration of stopping behavior was shorter compared to PDM-DN activation.
source: In few cases where wild-type larvae stopped, the average duration of stopping behavior was also shorter compared to the PDM-DN activation (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The probability of stopping was anti-correlated with tail speed in negative controls, but no dependence between stop probability and tail speed was found for PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae.
source: While we observed that the probability of stopping was anti-correlated with the tail speed in negative controls, no dependence between the stop probability and tail speed was found for PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae, highlighting the deterministic nature of the optogenetic activation phenotype (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3G.

claim: When subjected to a longer 20-s red-light flash, the majority of PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae remained in stopping mode for ~3 s, but the average tail speed gradually increased throughout the duration of the flash.
source: When subjected to a longer 20-s-red-light flash, the majority of PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae remained in stopping mode for ~3 s, but the average tail speed gradually increased throughout the duration of the flash (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, right panels).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The gradual increase in tail speed during prolonged PDM-DN activation indicated a failure to sustain stopping behavior, suggesting adaptation of the PDM-DN neuron or circuit-level mechanisms that bypass stopping behavior over longer durations.
source: This gradual increase in tail speed indicated a failure to sustain stopping behavior, thereby suggesting an adaptation of the PDM-DN neuron in response to persistent optogenetic activation or circuit-level mechanisms that bypass stopping behavior over longer durations (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, right panels).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PDM-DN produced a delayed increase in average head-angle speed peaking at ~3 s into the light activation.
source: Unlike the parental controls, the optogenetic activation of PDM-DN produced a delayed increase in the average head-angle speed peaking at ~3 s into the light activation (Figure 3H, magenta trace and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae spent significantly more time sweeping their head throughout the light flash compared to parental controls.
source: In addition, PDM-DN>CsChrimson larvae spent significantly more time sweeping their head throughout the light flash compared to the parental controls (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Head-casting behavior induced by PDM-DN activation varied strongly across trials and animals.
source: Unlike the decrease in tail speed, head-casting behavior induced by PDM-DN activation varied strongly across trials and animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 4B and D)
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4B and D.

claim: The effect of PDM-DN on the control of head-casting dynamics is less direct than its inhibition of forward peristalsis.
source: and demonstrated a sensitivity to sensory experience (Figure 3—figure supplement 5). These results suggest that the effect of PDM-DN on the control of the head-casting dynamics is less direct than its inhibition of forward peristalsis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Unilateral activation of the PDM-DN neuron was sufficient to induce stopping and head-casting behaviors.
source: Optogenetic unilateral activation of the PDM-DN neuron was sufficient to induce stopping and head-casting behaviors (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, right panel).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: PDM-DN activation prolonged ongoing stops when the larva was engaged in head casting behavior.
source: PDM-DN activation prolonged the ongoing stop (mean duration of stops: 4.66 ± 0.35 s, Figure 3—figure supplement 3D, magenta).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3D.

claim: When exposed to the same pattern of light stimulation, parental controls engaged in head casting behavior switched to running after 1-2 head casts.
source: When exposed to the same pattern of light stimulation, parental controls engaged in head casting behavior switched to running after 1–2 head casts (mean duration of stops: 2.81 ± 0.11 s, Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D, black).
evidence: This is a result from control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: PDM-DN-evoked stopping behavior does not depend on the behavioral state of the larva.
source: These results argue that PDM-DN-evoked stopping behavior does not depend on the behavioral state of the larva.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: The sensory experience did not appear to affect the dynamics underlying switches from running to stopping modes elicited by optogenetic activation of PDM-DN.
source: While the sensory experience did not appear to affect the dynamics underlying switches from running to stopping modes elicited by optogenetic activation of PDM-DN (Figure 3J–K and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–B)
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments in odor gradients shown in Figures 3J-K and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A-B.

claim: The head-casting behavior of PDM-DN->CsChrimson larvae showed a remarkable sensitivity to the sensory experience preceding a light flash: during down-gradient runs, larvae were more likely to engage in vigorous head casts than during up-gradient runs.
source: the head-casting behavior of PDM-DN->CsChrimson larvae showed a remarkable sensitivity to the sensory experience preceding a light flash: during down-gradient runs, larvae were more likely to engage in vigorous head casts than during up-gradient runs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F–G and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A–B).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments in odor gradients shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F-G and Figure 3—figure supplement 5A-B.

claim: The fraction of time spent casting was higher during down-gradient runs than during up-gradient runs upon optogenetic activation of PDM-DN.
source: Accordingly, the fraction of time spent casting was higher during down-gradient runs than during up-gradient runs (Figure 3M).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments in odor gradients shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Larvae that were moving down-gradient had a higher probability of implementing a head cast upon PDM-DN activation than larvae moving up-gradient.
source: Upon optogenetic activation, larvae that were moving down-gradient had a higher probability of implementing a head cast upon PDM-DN activation than larvae moving up-gradient (Figure 3M and Figure 3—figure supplement 3G, magenta).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments in odor gradients shown in Figure 3M and Figure 3—figure supplement 3G.

claim: Negative controls responded to light flashes by engaging in head casts during both down-gradient and up-gradient runs, suggesting that the startle response elicited by the light flashes overrides the olfactory information.
source: Negative controls responded to light flashes by engaging in head casts during both down-gradient and up-gradient runs (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and G, black), suggesting that the startle response elicited by the light flashes override the olfactory information.
evidence: This is a result from control experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3E and G, with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Artificial activation of the activity of PDM-DN triggers deterministic pausing behavior while it can evoke turning behavior in an experience-dependent way.
source: In short, artificial activation of the activity of PDM-DN triggers deterministic pausing behavior while it can evoke turning behavior in an experience-dependent way.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the optogenetic experiments.

claim: Forward locomotion is underlain by repetitive cycles of wave-like peristaltic contractions starting from the most posterior segments and ending at the anterior segments.
source: Forward locomotion is underlain by repetitive cycles of wave-like peristaltic contractions starting from the most posterior segments and ending at the anterior segments (Heckscher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about larval locomotion supported by a citation.

claim: At the beginning of each peristaltic wave, the tail speed reaches its maximum due to a mechanism called visceral-piston phase.
source: At the beginning of each peristaltic wave, the tail speed reaches its maximum due to a mechanism called visceral-piston phase (Heckscher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a fact about larval locomotion supported by a citation.

claim: When the wave terminates in the head region, the body of the larva is fully extended and its length reaches its maximal amplitude.
source: When the wave terminates in the head (anterior) region, the body of the larva is fully extended and its length reaches its maximal amplitude (Figure 4A, top panel).
evidence: This is an observation about larval locomotion shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The peristaltic wave cycle is defined as the period between a peak in tail speed and the subsequent peak in body length.
source: Based on this phenomenology, the peristaltic wave cycle is defined as the period between a peak (maximum) in tail speed and the subsequent peak in body length.
evidence: This is a definition used in the analysis of locomotion.

claim: The state of the peristaltic wave is described as an angle ranging from 0 (posterior end) to 360 (anterior end) degrees.
source: Given the cyclic nature of peristalsis, we described the state of the wave as an angle ranging from 0 (posterior end) to 360 (anterior end) degrees (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a definition used in the analysis of locomotion shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PDM-DN was followed by a steep decrease in tail speed, indicative of stopping behavior, regardless of the phase of the wave at which activation occurred.
source: In all cases, optogenetic activation of PDM-DN was followed by a steep decrease in tail speed, indicative of stopping behavior.
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments analyzing the effect on different phases of the peristaltic wave.

claim: The minimum of the average tail speed was observed ~1 s after the onset of the light flash.
source: The minimum of the average tail speed was observed ~1 s after the onset of the light flash (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Following optogenetic activation of PDM-DN, the average body length kept increasing steadily up to a maximum value independent of the phase at which the gain-of-function was implemented.
source: Following optogenetic activation of PDM-DN, the average body length kept increasing steadily up to a maximum value independent of the phase at which the gain-of-function was implemented.
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments.

claim: During the light flash, the larva remained fully extended for a couple of seconds before gradually relaxing.
source: During the light flash, the larva remained fully extended for a couple of seconds before gradually relaxing (Figure 4C, top inset).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PDM-DN activation does not result in an immediate freeze of peristalsis, but rather allows the conclusion of the ongoing wave at the time of the flash and suppresses the initiation of subsequent waves.
source: Together, these observations reveal that PDM-DN activation does not result in an immediate freeze of peristalsis, but rather that it allows the conclusion of the ongoing wave at the time of the flash and suppresses the initiation of subsequent waves.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of tail speed and body length during optogenetic activation.

claim: When PDM-DN was activated during the late phase of the wave, the ongoing wave continued and terminated at the most anterior segments; subsequent waves were suppressed.
source: When PDM-DN was activated during the late phase of the wave (denticle band displacement at segments A1-A3), the ongoing wave continued and terminated at the most anterior segments; subsequent waves were suppressed (Figure 4Ei).
evidence: This is a result from experiments tracking segmental contractions shown in Figure 4Ei.

claim: When PDM-DN activation coincided with the front of the wave activity at segment A4 or earlier, the wave either stopped immediately without propagating to anterior segments or it terminated at the most anterior segments; in either case, subsequent waves were blocked.
source: When PDM-DN activation coincided with the front of the wave activity at segment A4 or earlier, the wave either stopped immediately without propagating to anterior segments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) or it terminated at the most anterior segments (Figure 4Eii). In either case, subsequent waves were blocked.
evidence: This is a result from experiments tracking segmental contractions shown in Figure 4Eii and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: When the activation of PDM-DN coincided with the initial phase of the wave, the ongoing wave prematurely ceased before it reached the hinge point and the subsequent wave was also blocked.
source: When the activation of PDM-DN coincided with the initial phase of the wave (denticle band displacement at segment A7), a striking phenotype was observed: the ongoing wave prematurely ceased before it reached the hinge point (denticle band displacement at segment A4) (Figure 4Eiii, but see Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and the subsequent wave was also blocked.
evidence: This is a result from experiments tracking segmental contractions shown in Figure 4Eiii and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When optogenetic activation of PDM-DN coincided with the peristaltic wave at thoracic segments, subsequent waves could not be initiated while PDM-DN remained active.
source: Finally, when optogenetic activation of PDM-DN coincided with the peristaltic wave at thoracic segments, subsequent waves could not be initiated while PDM-DN remained active (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is a result from experiments tracking segmental contractions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Artificial activation of PDM-DN is capable of terminating the peristaltic wave before but not after the hinge segment A4.
source: Together, these observations suggest that artificial activation of PDM-DN is capable of terminating the peristaltic wave before but not after the hinge segment A4.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments tracking segmental contractions.

claim: Isolated larval CNS devoid of sensory input can still produce rhythmic patterns of motor-neuron activity (fictive locomotion) with coordinated segmental activity similar to muscle contractions in intact larvae.
source: Isolated larval CNS devoid of sensory input can still produce rhythmic patterns of motor-neuron activity (fictive locomotion) with coordinated segmental activity similar to muscle contractions in intact larvae (Lemon et al., 2015; Pulver et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a well-established fact about isolated CNS preparations supported by citations.

claim: Periodic sequences of motor-neuron activity associated with forward locomotion were observed in isolated CNS preparations.
source: Periodic sequences of motor-neuron activity associated with forward locomotion were observed in isolated CNS preparations (Figure 4G, image sequence).
evidence: This is a result from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Motor-neuron activity started in the most posterior segments (A7) and sequentially progressed to the most anterior segment A1, consistent with normal patterns of muscle contractions.
source: Consistent with normal patterns of muscle contractions, motor-neuron activity started in the most posterior segments (A7) and sequentially progressed to the most anterior segment A1 (dashed line labeled as F in Figure 4G, right panel).
evidence: This is a result from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The frequency of wave generation in isolated nervous systems was found to be ~5-10 times slower than during intact larval locomotion.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Berni, 2015; Pulver et al., 2015), the frequency of wave generation was found to be ~5–10 times slower in isolated nervous system than during intact larval locomotion.
evidence: This is an observation from calcium imaging experiments supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When the onset of PDM-DN activation coincided with the beginning of a wave, the wave terminated at the hinge point (A4).
source: When the onset of the PDM-DN activation coincided with the beginning of a wave, the wave terminated at the hinge point (A4) (Figure 4G, right panel)
evidence: This is a result from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The initiation of subsequent waves was severely suppressed upon PDM-DN activation.
source: The initiation of subsequent waves was severely suppressed.
evidence: This is a result from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The number of waves strongly decreased after the flash compared to controls without optogenetic stimulation of PDM-DN.
source: We found that the number of waves strongly decreased after the flash compared to controls without optogenetic stimulation of PDM-DN (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a result from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4H.

claim: PDM-DN is likely to induce pausing behavior by inhibiting the initiation of forward peristaltic waves in the posterior segments.
source: By investigating the effects of PDM-DN activation on segmental contractions and motor-neuron activity, we concluded that PDM-DN is likely to induce pausing behavior by inhibiting the initiation of forward peristaltic waves in the posterior segments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments on segmental contractions and motor-neuron activity.

claim: The circuitry involved in the control of the propagation of forward peristaltic waves includes a network of segmentally repeated excitatory premotor neurons called A27h.
source: The circuitry involved in the control of the propagation of forward peristaltic waves include a network of segmentally repeated excitatory premotor neurons called A27h (Fushiki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a fact about the premotor circuit supported by a citation.

claim: A27h excites motor neurons in the same segment, thereby promoting the contraction of longitudinal muscles involved in forward locomotion.
source: A27h excites motor neurons in the same segment, thereby promoting the contraction of longitudinal muscles involved in forward locomotion (Kohsaka et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a fact about A27h function supported by a citation.

claim: The A27h neurons of a given segment excite inhibitory GDL neurons in the adjacent anterior segment, which in turn suppress the activity of the A27h neurons in the same segment.
source: In addition, the A27h neurons of a given segment excite inhibitory GDL neurons in the adjacent anterior segment. In turn, the GDL neurons suppress the activity of the A27h neurons in the same segment.
evidence: This is a fact about the A27h-GDL circuit.

claim: A27h activity in a given segment leads to the contraction of the muscles in that segment while relaxing the muscles in the adjacent anterior segment by activating inhibitory GDL neurons.
source: Therefore, A27h activity in a given segment leads to the contraction of the muscles in that segment while relaxing the muscles in the adjacent anterior segment by activating inhibitory GDL neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the function of the A27h-GDL circuit.

claim: The connectivity pattern of the A27h neurons suggests that a mechanism based on the propagation of a wave of excitation-inhibition forms the pattern-generator-like mechanism underlying the propagation of forward waves of muscle contraction.
source: The connectivity pattern of the A27h neurons suggests that a mechanism based on the propagation of a wave of excitation-inhibition forms the pattern-generator-like mechanism underlying the propagation of forward waves of muscle contraction (Pehlevan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the A27h connectivity supported by a citation.

claim: PDM-DN must act on the activity of the A27h network because activation of PDM-DN produces near-deterministic stops of forward locomotion.
source: Since the activation of PDM-DN produces near-deterministic stops of forward locomotion (Figure 3E–F and Video 1), we speculated that PDM-DN must act on the activity of the A27h network.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the behavioral phenotype and knowledge of the premotor circuit.

claim: EM connectivity data showed that PDM-DN is connected to different types of premotor neurons through a set of descending neurons in the SEZ region.
source: EM connectivity data showed that PDM-DN is connected to different types of premotor neurons through a set of descending neurons in the SEZ region (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplements 1C and 2C–D).
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: EM reconstruction revealed that PDM-DN is connected to the A27h premotor network through a descending neuron named SEZ-DN1.
source: EM reconstruction revealed that PDM-DN is connected to the A27h premotor network through a descending neuron named SEZ-DN1.
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction.

claim: SEZ-DN1 has its dendritic arbors in the SEZ region and projects its axon to the posterior abdominal segments of the VNC.
source: SEZ-DN1 has its dendritic arbors in the SEZ region. This neuron projects its axon to the posterior abdominal segments of the VNC (Figure 5C, left and middle panels).
evidence: This is an anatomical observation shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SEZ-DN1 exclusively targets the A27h neurons located in the most posterior segments of the VNC.
source: As shown in the Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, SEZ-DN1 exclusively targets the A27h neurons located in the most posterior segments of the VNC.
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: No synaptic connections are observed between SEZ-DN1 and A27h neurons in the segments anterior to the hinge point defined by segment A4.
source: Remarkably, no synaptic connections are observed between the SEZ-DN1 and A27h neuron in the segments anterior to the hinge point defined by segment A4 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction.

claim: A Gal4 line was identified that specifically labeled the SEZ-DN1 neuron.
source: By screening the expression patterns of Gal4 driver lines (Li et al., 2014; Dionne et al., 2018), we identified a Gal4 line that specifically labeled the SEZ-DN1 neuron (R75C02, Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes the identification of a genetic tool shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Immunostaining showed that PDM-DN is unlikely to express GABA or glutamate.
source: Immunostaining for GABA and glutamate together with the labeling of PDM-DN (PDM-DN>CsChrimson::mVenus) showed that PDM-DN is unlikely to express GABA or glutamate (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a result from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PDM-DN labeling showed co-localization with choline acetyltransferase, suggesting that PDM-DN is cholinergic.
source: By contrast, PDM-DN labeling showed co-localization with choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), the enzyme necessary for the synthesis of acetylcholine (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A). This result suggested that PDM-DN was cholinergic.
evidence: This is a result from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RNAi knock-down of ChAT abolished the PDM-DN gain-of-function phenotype.
source: RNAi knock-down of ChaT abolished the PDM-DN gain-of-function phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that acetylcholine release is necessary for PDM-DN-evoked pauses.
evidence: This is a result from RNAi experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Acetylcholine release is necessary for PDM-DN-evoked pauses.
source: indicating that acetylcholine release is necessary for PDM-DN-evoked pauses.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the RNAi experiments.

claim: The fact that PDM-DN is likely to be a cholinergic excitatory neuron implied that SEZ-DN1 must be inhibitory to block the activity of the A27h neuron.
source: The fact that PDM-DN is likely to be a cholinergic excitatory neuron implied that SEZ-DN1 must be inhibitory to block the activity of the A27h neuron.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the neurotransmitter identity of PDM-DN and the behavioral phenotype.

claim: Immunostaining for GABA with the labeling of SEZ-DN1 led to co-localization at the level of soma of this neuron.
source: Accordingly, immunostaining for the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA with the labeling of SEZ-DN1 led to co-localization at the level of soma of this neuron (Figure 5C, right panel).
evidence: This is a result from immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the SEZ-DN1 neuron led to transitions from runs to stop/casts similar to PDM-DN.
source: Furthermore, optogenetic activation of the SEZ-DN1 neuron led to transitions from runs to stop/casts similar to PDM-DN (Figure 5D–E, Video 3).
evidence: This is a result from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 5D-E and Video 3.

claim: SEZ-DN1 is a GABAergic neuron with an inhibitory effect on the A27h network of premotor neurons restricted to the posterior segments where forward waves of peristaltic contractions are initiated.
source: We conclude that SEZ-DN1 is a GABAergic neuron with an inhibitory effect on the A27h network of premotor neurons restricted to the posterior segments where forward waves of peristaltic contractions are initiated.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunostaining, optogenetic, and EM reconstruction data.

claim: PDM-DN employs distinct SEZ and abdominal interneurons to differentially regulate stopping and head casting/turning behaviors.
source: EM reconstruction and functional analysis revealed that PDM-DN employs distinct SEZ and abdominal interneurons to differentially regulate stopping and head casting/turning behaviors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the EM reconstruction and functional experiments.

claim: In segments A6 and A7, the A27h neurons received bilateral inputs from the SEZ-DN1 descending neuron, which itself received direct bilateral input from the PDM-DN neuron.
source: In segments A6 and A7, the A27h neurons received bilateral inputs from the SEZ-DN1 descending neuron (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), which itself received direct bilateral input from the PDM-DN neuron.
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The finding that A27h neurons located in segments anterior from A4 were unaffected by PDM-DN activity corroborated the absence of connectivity between SEZ-DN1 and A27 neurons in the abdominal segments anterior to A4.
source: Our finding that the A27h neurons located in segments anterior from A4 were unaffected by PDM-DN activity corroborated the absence of connectivity between SEZ-DN1 and A27 neurons in the abdominal segments anterior to A4.
evidence: This is a conclusion that integrates functional and anatomical data.

claim: PDM-DN has two additional post-synaptic partners in the SEZ that innervate known elements of the premotor system: SEZ-LN1 and SEZ-DN2.
source: PDM-DN has two additional post-synaptic partners in the SEZ that innervate known elements of the premotor system. First, SEZ-LN1 (Figure 5A, gray color and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B) is a local interneuron in the SEZ.
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: SEZ-LN1 outputs on a premotor circuit that controls a set of motor neurons (RP2, RP3 and RP4) in segments T1, A1 and A2.
source: SEZ-LN1 outputs on a premotor circuit that controls a set of motor neurons (RP2, RP3 and RP4) in segments T1, A1 and A2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: SEZ-LN1 connects contralaterally to RP2s and ipsilaterally to RP3 and RP4s.
source: Interestingly, SEZ-LN1 connects contralaterally to RP2s and ipsilaterally to RP3 and RP4s.
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction.

claim: Asymmetrical contraction of dorsal and ventral muscles might contribute to the pattern of head sweeps elicited by optogenetic activation of PDM-DN.
source: We speculate that asymmetrical contraction of dorsal and ventral muscles might contribute to the pattern of head sweeps elicited by optogenetic activation of PDM-DN.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the connectivity of SEZ-LN1.

claim: SEZ-DN2 directly innervates premotor neurons upstream from the motor neurons of the prothoracic accessory nerve (PaN).
source: We identified a second descending neuron in the SEZ, named SEZ-DN2. This neuron directly innervates premotor neurons upstream from the motor neurons of the prothoracic accessory nerve (PaN) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C)
evidence: This is a result from EM reconstruction shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: PaN motor neurons control head tilting movements during feeding behavior.
source: — a set of neurons that controls head tilting movements during feeding behavior (Hückesfeld et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a fact about PaN motor neurons supported by a citation.

claim: It is possible that the SEZ-DN2 neurons provide input to the PaN motor neurons, which execute head tilting maneuvers that contribute to the head-scanning routine preceding the implementation of turns.
source: In particular, it is possible that the SEZ-DN2 neurons provide input to the PaN motor neurons, which execute head tilting maneuvers — a behavior that contributes to the head-scanning routine preceding the implementation of turns (Green et al., 1983; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the connectivity of SEZ-DN2 and known behavior.

claim: When SEZ-DN1 gain of function took place after the peristaltic wave had crossed the hinge point (segment A4), the wave tended to propagate up to the most anterior segment where it terminated, and subsequent waves were inhibited.
source: When SEZ-DN1 gain of function took place after the peristaltic wave had crossed the hinge point (segment A4), the wave tended to propagate up to the most anterior segment where it terminated. Subsequent waves were inhibited (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a result from experiments tracking segmental contractions shown in Figure 6A.

claim: SEZ-DN1 optogenetic activation was sufficient to block the propagation of forward wave when the wave was still located in the region posterior to the hinge point.
source: Consistent with the effects of gain-of-function manipulations of PDM-DN, SEZ-DN1 optogenetic activation was sufficient to block the propagation of forward wave when the wave was still located in the region posterior to the hinge point (Figure 6Aiii and B).
evidence: This is a result from experiments tracking segmental contractions shown in Figure 6Aiii and B.

claim: Spontaneous forward waves of activity in motor neurons of the VNC were suppressed upon optogenetic activation of SEZ-DN1.
source: Spontaneous forward waves of activity in motor neurons of the VNC were suppressed upon optogenetic activation of SEZ-DN1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a result from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The activation of SEZ-DN1 drastically reduced the number of fictive waves of motor neuron activity observed before and during the light flash.
source: As reported in Figure 6D, the activation of SEZ-DN1 drastically reduced the number of fictive waves of motor neuron activity observed before and during the light flash.
evidence: This is a result from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 6D.

claim: PDM-DN has an excitatory effect on the activity of SEZ-DN1.
source: Using calcium imaging, we corroborated the idea that PDM-DN has an excitatory effect on the activity of SEZ-DN1.
evidence: This is a conclusion from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: The activity of PDM-DN excited neural activity in the axons of SEZ-DN1.
source: By expressing CsChrimson in PDM-DN and imaging the activity of SEZ-DN1 with GCaMP6f, we observed that the activity of PDM-DN excited neural activity in the axons of SEZ-DN1 (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: This is a result from calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: A model is validated where PDM-DN activates SEZ-DN1, which in turn inhibits the activity of the A27h pre-motor system.
source: These experiments validate a model where PDM-DN activates SEZ-DN1, which in turn inhibits the activity of the A27h pre-motor system.
evidence: This is a conclusion that integrates multiple lines of experimental evidence.
